title: How do you determine what model to use for what task?
author: Will_X_Intent
selftext:
So I am using Claude mostly.  Opus is just so damned smart that I am tempted to use it for everything.  But that's probably overkill, especially if you are talking about using Opus 4.8 Max Thinking.  I think using the higher token usage models for the hardcore design work might be worth it, because clarify and understanding are of paramount importance.  But once we got the idea down, do you think I could downgrade without meaningful loss in performance?  And when it comes in actually turning those ideas into code/ gameplay systems, what should the minimum model be?  

With Opus 4.7, everything set as high as it would go, I would run out of tokens in about 4 hours of focused work.  This is when we are actually working with code or blueprints.  Now Opus 4.8 is out with all these options, and I don't know how I should use it.

comments.author: TheBigDamAdventure
comments.body: Opus is definitely much better than sonnet. I have adjusted the intensity down to medium to try to save some effort. I notice Claude does create lesser agents in haiku and sonnet to do subtasks (like search through your git). Unless it's real grunt work, I always use the highest model, put it in planning mode first and ask it to ask clarifying questions, then once the plan is in good shape, implement. Also starting new sessions is the best way to save effort. I read somewhere that keeping work in the same session wastes alot of token to reread the whole session, and I think this is true. Starting new sessions saves a lot of tokens, the only advantage of staying in a session is staying in a git branch (if you don't want to merge it into your main branch)

comments.author: SquirrelTomahawk
comments.body:
Don't know.. I was banging my head against the wall with Claude for months. Switched to Codex for the hell of it and it's been plowing through my workload and debugging a lot of issues that Claude was hallucinating with for months. Definitely felt a huge momentum shift but maybe I'm just taking the lessons I learned while using Claude and applying it in Codex. 

I think everyone has different experiences as of right now, it's a mixed bag.

comments.author: teamharder
comments.body:
This is a copy/pasta of an explanation about my skill.  
  
I type /game-dev and I tell Opus to add VFX to my characters skill > he wakes up, reads the skill, sees Vfx tasks should go to the VFX sub-agent > Opus spools up a cheaper sub-agent and says "here's the task, go read this .MD to know how to do your job" > Opus doesn't read the "employee manual" for that job, he just says "there's the bookshelf, go read it" > employee reads the hand off from CEO and the manual, does the work and reports back to the CEO > CEO verifies the work and reports to me. 

The question is "why not just have the smart CEO do everything? Delegation like that seems overly complex and cumbersome". Sure, the CEO burns tokens handing out jobs and I use more tokens overall. BUT those tokens are distributed across many agents. I use Opus 1 million token context models and I never go above 400-500k tokens with that one window, even in a 4-6 hour overnight session. Each sub agent burns 50-200k tokens, but that never clutters the main window or each other. These models become more expensive and dumb as you get closer to their token limit.

Also, the employee gets a clean and simple task every time. No extra crap to distract him. If he does a really bad job? Instead of working further with a bad employee, the CEO fires him and hires another. If models make a mistake once, they're likely to make it again.
